stem: What is the scientific name of the white rhinoceros?

options.content: *Ceratotherium simum*
*Diceros bicornis*
*Loxodonta africana*
*Hippopotamus amphibius*

explanation: White rhino: *Ceratotherium simum*; black rhino: *Diceros bicornis*.

stem: What is the main aim of the CAMPFIRE programme?

options.content: To let communities benefit from wildlife so they conserve it
To move all people out of areas where wildlife is found
options.rationale: CAMPFIRE works with communities, not by removing them.

options.content: To ban hunting of every wild animal species in Zimbabwe
options.rationale: CAMPFIRE income has often come from regulated hunting.

options.content: To regulate pollution from mines and factories across the country
options.rationale: That is a role of EMA.

explanation: CAMPFIRE shares income from wildlife (tourism, hunting) with communities, giving them an incentive to protect it.

stem: Which is a role of the Environmental Management Agency (EMA)?

options.content: Setting the international rules on trade in ivory
options.rationale: International trade is regulated through CITES.

options.content: Publishing the global Red List of threatened species
Sharing hunting revenue with rural district councils
Reviewing environmental impact assessments

explanation: EMA enforces environmental law, including impact assessments, pollution control and environmental education.

stem: Why is dehorning used to protect white rhinos?

options.content: It stops the horn regrowing, so the rhino is protected for life
options.rationale: The keratin horn regrows; dehorning must be repeated.

options.content: It makes the rhino more aggressive, so poachers keep away
It removes the horn, so the rhino is less valuable to poachers
It allows vets to fit radio collars more easily
options.rationale: Collars are not fitted to horns.

explanation: A dehorned rhino offers little reward to poachers; the horn regrows, so it is repeated every year or two.

stem: Why does the population of a large, slow-breeding mammal such as the elephant take a long time to recover after heavy poaching?

options.content: Elephants cannot breed until they have reached about 50 years of age
options.rationale: Elephants mature far earlier than this.

options.content: Poached elephants are usually the young calves rather than the adults
options.rationale: Poachers target adults with large tusks.

options.content: Long gestation and long gaps between calves give a low birth rate
Elephants can only breed when they have been moved to a sanctuary

explanation: Gestation is about 22 months and calves come about every 4-5 years, so numbers rise slowly.

stem: Elephants in a park are concentrated near artificial water points in the dry season. Which effect is most likely near the water points?

options.content: Woodland thickens because elephant dung fertilises the soil
options.rationale: Damage outweighs any fertilising effect near water.

options.content: Species diversity of plants rises because of extra water
options.rationale: Heavy use usually lowers plant diversity.

options.content: Grass cover increases because elephants avoid eating grass
options.rationale: Elephants eat large amounts of grass.

options.content: Woodland is damaged as trees are pushed over and debarked

explanation: High elephant density exceeds the local carrying capacity; trees are broken, uprooted and debarked faster than they regrow.
hints: What happens when many large browsers stay in one area?

stem: Under CITES, what is the general rule for species listed on Appendix I?

options.content: Trade is allowed with permits showing it does no harm
International commercial trade in them is not permitted
Hunting them within their home country is always illegal
options.rationale: CITES regulates international trade, not domestic hunting.

options.content: They are protected only inside national parks
options.rationale: CITES is about trade between countries.

explanation: Appendix I: species threatened with extinction; commercial international trade banned. Appendix II: trade controlled by permits.
hints: CITES is about trade between countries.

stem: Which argument is used by those who oppose any legal sale of stockpiled ivory?

options.content: Ivory from natural deaths has no value to buyers anywhere in the world
Legal ivory may raise demand and help launder illegal ivory
options.rationale: Correct: concerns about laundering and demand.

options.content: Money from sales could not legally be spent on any form of conservation
options.rationale: Proponents propose using it for conservation.

options.content: Elephant populations in southern Africa are all far below carrying capacity
options.rationale: This is not the argument used; some are locally high.

explanation: Opponents argue that legal sales can increase demand and make illegal ivory harder to detect; supporters argue that sales of stockpiles could fund conservation.
hints: Think about what happens to demand and enforcement.

stem: Rhino horn is made of keratin, the same protein found in hair and nails.
explanation: True. This is why it regrows after dehorning.

stem: The white rhinoceros is mainly a browser that feeds on the leaves of shrubs.
explanation: False. The white rhino is a grazer with a wide, square lip; the black rhino is the browser with a hooked lip.

stem: Match each organisation or agreement with its role.

right.content: Shares wildlife income with rural communities
Regulates international trade in wildlife products
Enforces environmental law and impact assessments

explanation: CITES (international trade), EMA (environmental law), CAMPFIRE (community benefits), ZimParks (parks and wildlife).

explanation: 2310 ÷ 1400 = 1.65 elephants per km². Dividing area by number gives the area per elephant instead.

stem: An illustrative sanctuary held 52 white rhinos. In one year 9 were poached and no calves were born. Calculate the percentage decrease in the population. Give your answer to one decimal place.
explanation:
1. Population after the losses $= 52 - 9 = 43$.
2. Percentage decrease $= \dfrac{9}{52} \times 100 = 17.3\%$.
3. Dividing by 43 instead of 52 gives 20.9%, which uses the wrong base.
workedSolution:
1. Population after the losses $= 52 - 9 = 43$.
2. Percentage decrease $= \dfrac{9}{52} \times 100 = 17.3\%$.
3. Dividing by 43 instead of 52 gives 20.9%, which uses the wrong base.
hints: Use the starting population as the base.

stem: Explain how the CAMPFIRE programme is intended to help conserve elephants in communal areas.

points.description: Communities (through rural district councils) are given authority over wildlife on their land
Income from safari hunting quotas and tourism is shared with communities
Money funds local projects / household income, so wildlife is seen as valuable rather than only a pest
Communities therefore have an incentive to protect wildlife habitat, report poachers and tolerate some crop damage

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: CAMPFIRE gives rural district councils, on behalf of communities, authority over wildlife on communal land. Income from regulated safari hunting and photographic tourism is shared with the communities and used for schools, clinics, boreholes or cash dividends. Because elephants bring benefits, people see them as a resource rather than just a pest, so they have an incentive to keep wildlife habitat, report poachers and tolerate some crop damage.

explanation: Benefits → incentive → protection.
hints: Why would a farmer protect an animal that eats his crops?

stem: Discuss the arguments for and against culling elephants in an area where their numbers exceed the carrying capacity of the habitat.

points.description: For: high densities destroy woodland, reducing habitat for other species / biodiversity
For: reduces human-wildlife conflict and crop raiding / may provide meat and income for communities
Against: ethical objections to killing intelligent, social animals; culling disrupts family groups
Against: may harm tourism and the country's image; alternatives exist (translocation, closing water points, contraception, corridors)
Balanced conclusion: decision should depend on monitoring data and alternatives considered first / numbers may fall naturally in drought

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Supporters of culling argue that too many elephants destroy woodland, reducing habitat and food for other species and lowering biodiversity, and that fewer elephants means less crop raiding, while meat and income can benefit communities. Opponents argue that killing intelligent, social animals is unethical and disrupts family groups, that it may damage tourism and the country's reputation, and that alternatives such as translocation, closing some artificial water points, contraception and corridors to other areas exist. A balanced view is that decisions should be based on careful monitoring of both elephants and vegetation, with alternatives tried first.

explanation: Arguments on both sides, attributed to groups, plus a conclusion.
hints: Consider the habitat, people, ethics and alternatives.

stem: Suggest three economic benefits to Zimbabwe of conserving elephants and rhinos.

points.description: Tourism brings foreign currency
Jobs in lodges, as guides and rangers / income for local communities through CAMPFIRE
Revenue from regulated trophy hunting or park fees funds conservation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Wildlife tourism earns foreign currency for the country. It provides jobs in lodges and as guides and rangers, and CAMPFIRE passes income to rural communities. Park fees and regulated hunting generate revenue that can be used for conservation.

explanation: Tourism, employment and revenue.
hints: Who pays to see or hunt wildlife?

stem:
Illustrative data for a wildlife area bordering farmland in the Zambezi valley.

| Year | 2011 | 2014 | 2017 | 2020 | 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elephants counted | 820 | 905 | 990 | 1060 | 1150 |
| Crop-raiding incidents reported | 34 | 41 | 57 | 66 | 79 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in elephants from 2011 to 2023. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the relationship between elephant numbers and crop raiding.

points.description: As elephant numbers increase (820 to 1150), crop-raiding incidents increase (34 to 79): positive correlation
Raids increase proportionally faster than elephants (more than double, while elephants rose by about 40%)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Both increase together: elephants rose from 820 to 1150 and raids from 34 to 79, a positive correlation. Raids more than doubled while elephants increased by about 40%, so raids rose proportionally faster.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why crop raiding increased faster than elephant numbers.

points.description: As numbers approach carrying capacity, food in the wildlife area becomes scarcer, so more elephants seek food on farms
Farmland may have expanded towards the park boundary / drought reduced natural food

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: As the population approaches the carrying capacity, natural food becomes scarce, so a greater proportion of elephants leave to feed on crops. Farmland may also have expanded closer to the boundary.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest two measures that could reduce human-elephant conflict without killing elephants.

points.description: Fences (electric) / buffer crops such as chilli or beehive fences / early warning and guarding
Land-use planning to keep fields away from corridors / translocation / compensation or CAMPFIRE income to offset losses

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Electric or beehive fences and chilli barriers can deter elephants from fields. Land-use planning can keep fields away from elephant corridors, and CAMPFIRE income or compensation can offset losses.

explanation: Positive relationship; scarcity near carrying capacity; non-lethal measures.

stem: A newspaper reports that a conservancy in the lowveld plans to dehorn all its rhinos, increase ranger patrols and translocate ten rhinos to a new sanctuary in another province.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why dehorning must be repeated every one to two years.

points.description: Horn is keratin and regrows continuously
Regrown horn again becomes valuable to poachers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rhino horn is made of keratin and grows continuously from its base, so after a year or two there is enough horn to attract poachers again.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give three biological advantages of translocating ten rhinos to a new sanctuary.

points.description: Spreads the population so one poaching or disease event cannot kill all the rhinos
Reduces density / competition for food in the conservancy, raising breeding rate
Starts a new breeding population / allows gene flow when animals are moved between populations

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Splitting the population means a single disease outbreak or poaching gang cannot destroy all the rhinos. It reduces density and competition for grazing, which can increase breeding. It also starts a new breeding population and, when animals are moved between populations, maintains genetic diversity.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which organisation would review an environmental impact assessment if the new sanctuary required a large dam?

options.content: The CITES Secretariat in Geneva
The Environmental Management Agency
The CAMPFIRE committee of the district
The IUCN Red List authority
options.rationale: IUCN assesses extinction risk of species.

parts.explanation: EMA reviews environmental impact assessments in Zimbabwe.

explanation: Dehorning, translocation and EMA's role.
